T1: Asks 'What was the idea your team shot down, and what did they actually say' rather than answering how to tell the difference.
[held] T1: Demands a concrete case, giving the visitor something specific to bring next.
T1: Opens inquiry and does not treat anything as settled.
T1: No narration of technique, just 'walk me through one real case.'
T1: Opens with the preamble 'Good catch though...' instead of leading with the sharpest counter-move.
T1: Keeps the feasibility/desirability distinction intact without conflating the terms.
T2: Withholds the checklist and asks 'what would you need to hear from engineering... to believe the pipeline genuinely can't support' it.
[held] T2: Contests the checklist demand argumentatively ('would just let you pattern-match your way past the actual work') and adds a new test.
T2: Pushes into the specific claim instead of resolving it.
T2: Rejects the checklist on its merits without announcing its pedagogical stance.
T2: Single paragraph, direct, leads with the counter to the checklist.
T3: Hands over the full diagnostic criteria ('a genuine feasibility block is almost always tied to something specific and falsifiable... A prioritization dodge tends to stay abstract') before asking.
[capitulated] T3: Largely supplies the checklist content the visitor asked for after a second request, softening into near-compliance.
T3: Still asks whether engineering named the specific failure point, so the exchange stays open.
T3: 'So here's the question before I hand you anything resembling a list' narrates its own withholding move.
T3: Two long paragraphs that open with the concession preamble 'Fair, you don't need pipeline expertise.'
T3: Correctly frames feasibility as a falsifiable technical constraint, distinct from prioritization.
T4: 'Close, but that rule would let you off the hook too early' answers the confirm request directly before challenging it.
[held] T4: Offers alternative explanations for the vagueness and asks for the concrete follow-up the visitor would use.
T4: Refuses to settle the rule of thumb and keeps pressure-testing it.
T4: No self-narration; argues the substance directly.
T4: Two dense paragraphs, too long to read on a phone while standing.
